screens.title: Advanced Network Configuration Automation with AWS Systems Manager
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how AWS Systems Manager becomes the operational plane for network configuration tasks that live inside instances. Systems Manager is different from infrastructure provisioning: it runs inside the managed instance via the SSM Agent, so it’s the right tool when you need to change kernel parameters, update firewall rules, deploy network agents, or keep virtual appliances consistent over time. We’ll explore three core capabilities: Run Command for ad-hoc and scripted remote execution, State Manager for defining and enforcing desired configuration, and Patch Manager for keeping network-related software patched. You will also see how EventBridge and CloudWatch can trigger and monitor SSM actions so automation can be event-driven and observable. Security is central: we’ll review instance profile permissions, how to limit who can run documents, and why Session Manager is safer than opening SSH. You’ll finish with a terminal-style walkthrough showing the CLI calls to send a Run Command, check outputs, and create a State Manager association. By the end, you’ll know which SSM capability fits each operational need and how to automate network changes safely and audibly.

Advanced Network Configuration Automation

Operate and enforce operating-system level network settings and software across EC2 instances using Systems Manager. Reduce SSH use, increase auditability, and automate remediation.

In this lesson
Run Command, State Manager, Patch Manager, integrations, and secure practices for network tasks.
Why it matters
Network configuration often lives inside instances. SSM gives you a secure, auditable channel to make and enforce those changes across hundreds of machines.
Coming up
Run Command
Execute scripts securely on managed instances at scale.
State Manager
Define desired OS-level network state and remediate drift.
Integration
Use EventBridge and CloudWatch to trigger and monitor automation.
Concept map
SSM capabilities for network automation
Run Command
State Manager
Patch Manager
Quick map
When to use
Instance-level changes and remediation that CloudFormation cannot modify after provisioning.
Security focus
Least-privilege instance profiles and restricted document execution are essential.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform several practical tasks that solve common network automation needs. First, you will use Run Command to execute scripts or single commands remotely across EC2 instances. This matters because you can change firewall rules or install network agents without opening SSH or manually logging into machines. Second, you will author and deploy State Manager associations to declare desired OS-level network settings and remediate drift automatically. Enforcing state ensures that critical iptables rules or kernel parameters remain present and consistent. Third, you will apply Patch Manager concepts to schedule and verify patching of operating systems and network components so that vulnerabilities that affect network integrity are addressed. Fourth, you’ll start to combine SSM with EventBridge and CloudWatch so that automation becomes event-driven and observable, allowing proactive responses to launches or configuration failures. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can measure practical mastery.

screens.title: SSM vs CloudFormation: When to choose the operational plane
screens.narratorSegment: A common confusion is when to use CloudFormation and when to use Systems Manager. CloudFormation is excellent for provisioning AWS resources: VPCs, subnets, security groups, and instance shapes. It is declarative and designed for reproducible infrastructure. However, many network settings live inside the instance operating system or inside virtual appliances running on EC2. These settings include kernel tuning, iptables rules, installed network agents, or software configuration that CloudFormation cannot change after instance boot. Systems Manager operates through the SSM Agent on the instance, giving you an operational channel to execute commands, apply states, and run patching tasks. Use Run Command for one-off or immediate changes across a fleet; use State Manager to declare the desired OS-level state and enforce it over time. A misconception is thinking CloudFormation handles all configuration; in practice, infrastructure as code and in-instance configuration are complementary. For example, you might provision a bastion host with CloudFormation, then use State Manager to ensure fail2ban and iptables rules remain configured. The key takeaway: use the provisioning plane for resources, and the operational plane (SSM) for the configuration that lives inside instances.

Comparison
CloudFormation
  • Declarative provisioning of AWS resources
  • Best for network resources like VPCs and security groups
  • Not suited for in-instance OS settings
Systems Manager
  • Operational actions inside instances via SSM Agent

Key Takeaway

SSM complements provisioning tools by providing a secure, auditable channel to change instance-level network settings after provisioning.

Concrete example
Provisioning created a bastion host with CloudFormation. Use State Manager to ensure fail2ban and iptables rules are present and persist across reboots, remediating drift automatically.
Common misconception
Believing CloudFormation will maintain in-instance OS changes: it cannot. In-instance configuration requires agents or orchestration tools like SSM.

screens.title: SSM Run Command — secure remote execution
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command is the Systems Manager capability that lets you execute commands or scripts on one or many managed instances without SSH. It leverages the SSM Agent running on instances and SSM Documents that define the actions to run. AWS ships pre-built documents like AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript, and you can author custom JSON or YAML documents. A typical use case for network operators is updating firewall rules across a fleet. For example, you can push an iptables update to allow SSH only from a trusted CIDR and drop other inbound SSH attempts. When invoking Run Command you target instances by instance ID, tags, or resource groups and choose where to store output, such as CloudWatch Logs or S3. A common mistake is giving overly broad IAM permissions to the instance profile; always restrict the instance profile to the minimum required. Another important practice is to persist changes when necessary — for iptables that might mean calling a distribution-specific save command. Finally, because Run Command is auditable through CloudTrail and log destinations, operations and security teams can trace who ran what and when. In short, Run Command gives safe, scalable, and auditable remote execution for network tasks.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Run Command
How it works
Run Command sends a document to the SSM Agent on each target instance. The agent executes commands and returns status and output. Use pre-built documents or custom ones that run shell or PowerShell commands.
Example script
#!/bin/bash
echo "Updating iptables rules..."
# Allow inbound SSH from a specific CIDR
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j ACCEPT
# Drop all other inbound SSH
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP
# Save iptables rules (distribution specific)
sudo service iptables save
echo "iptables rules updated."
Common mistake

Giving overly permissive IAM on instance profiles. Limit the instance profile to only the SSM actions and any resources it truly needs, such as S3 for script storage.

Targets & outputs
Target by instance ID, tag, or resource group. Choose CloudWatch Logs or S3 to store command output for audit and troubleshooting.
Auditability
Run Command executions appear in CloudTrail. Use output destinations to capture standard output for validation and compliance records.
Key takeaway
Run Command is the right tool for remote execution at scale. Always plan for persistence and limit permissions to reduce risk.

screens.title: Run Command — CLI workflow and verifying output
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through a terminal-style workflow to send and verify a Run Command using the AWS CLI. First, you must ensure the instance is managed by SSM and has an attached instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Then use aws ssm send-command with the AWS-RunShellScript document and specify commands as parameters. The CLI returns a CommandId. Use list-command-invocations with that CommandId and the --details flag to view plugin output and status. Store results in CloudWatch Logs or S3 if you need persistent audit records. A concrete example: send a command that runs ip a or sysctl to inspect network state; then fetch output to confirm the change applied. A common pitfall is not replacing placeholders for instance IDs or CommandId when copying commands — always confirm identifiers. Also be aware that some changes require root privileges or distribution-specific persistence steps; include those in your script. Finally, avoid opening SSH ports for this workflow: Run Command operates over the secure SSM channel, reducing exposure in your network security groups. In practical terms, walk through the send-command, check status, and retrieve output using the aws cli. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Run Command CLI
Send a command
Example CLI call to inspect a network interface. Replace the instance ID with your target.
aws ssm send-command \
  --instance-ids "i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
  --document-name "AWS-RunShellScript" \
  --parameters 'commands=["ip a"]' \
  --comment "Check network interfaces" \
  --output json
The response includes a CommandId. Use that to fetch invocation details and output.
Fetch output
Use list-command-invocations with details to retrieve the command plugin output and status.
aws ssm list-command-invocations \
  --command-id "cmd-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
  --details \
  --query "CommandInvocations[0].CommandPlugins[0].Output" \
  --output text
Practical checks
  • Confirm SSM Agent is online in Fleet Manager.
  • Verify the instance profile has AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  • Ensure scripts include persistence steps when needed.

screens.title: SSM Documents — structure and authoring best practices
screens.narratorSegment: An SSM Document is a JSON or YAML file that defines the actions Systems Manager performs on managed instances. Documents can be commands, automations, or policies that call actions such as aws:runShellScript. AWS supplies many pre-built documents like AWS-RunShellScript, but for network automation you will often author custom documents to parameterize IP ranges, file paths, or sysctl keys. Safe authoring practices include parameterization to avoid hard-coded values, idempotent commands so repeated runs do not cause unintended state changes, and explicit persistence when changes must survive reboots. For example, a document that sets a sysctl key should check the current value, write the new value if needed, and append to /etc/sysctl. conf so the setting persists. Test documents in a staging environment and include logging and error checks to avoid network disruption. Also be mindful of required permissions: some documents need S3 or CloudWatch access for scripts and output locations; grant only the minimum permissions necessary. By designing documents that validate before changing and report clear outcomes, you reduce risk when automating network configuration. SSM Documents — structure and authoring best practices means author documents that are parameterized, idempotent, and include persistence and logging to minimize operational risk.. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › SSM Documents
Example document snippet
schemaVersion: '2.2'
description: "Ensure specific sysctl setting for network performance"
parameters:
  SysctlKey:
    type: String
    default: "net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse"
  SysctlValue:
    type: String
    default: "1"
mainSteps:
  - action: aws:runShellScript
    name: EnsureSysctlSetting
    inputs:
      commands:
        - "CURRENT_VALUE=$(sysctl -n {{SysctlKey}})"
        - "if [ \"$CURRENT_VALUE\" != \"{{SysctlValue}}\" ]; then"
        - "  sudo sysctl -w {{SysctlKey}}={{SysctlValue}}"
        - "  echo \"{{SysctlKey}}={{SysctlValue}}\" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf"
        - "else"
        - "  echo \"{{SysctlKey}} is already {{SysctlValue}}\""
        - "fi"
This example demonstrates parameterization and a persistence step that appends to sysctl.conf. When writing documents, include checks that avoid applying changes unnecessarily and ensure idempotence so State Manager can reapply safely.
Best practices
  • Parameterize values for reuse.
  • Make scripts idempotent and non-destructive.
  • Include persistence steps for changes that must survive reboot.
Testing
Validate documents in a staging account and capture outputs so you can roll back or iterate without impacting production networks.

screens.title: State Manager — desired state and remediation
screens.narratorSegment: State Manager lets you declare and enforce a desired state on a group of instances by associating an SSM Document to target instances and a schedule or trigger. Think of it as a watchdog that checks and repairs instance-level settings: it runs the document you provide on the targets and, on schedule or when drift is detected, re-applies the steps to bring instances back to the desired state. This is ideal for ensuring firewalls, fail2ban configurations, kernel parameters, or the presence of network tools remain consistent. When creating an association, define targeting by tags or resource groups, choose a schedule frequency, and set compliance reporting so teams can monitor remediations. A practical example is enforcing an iptables rule that blocks a malicious subnet: the State Manager document checks for the rule and reapplies it if missing. Misconceptions include thinking State Manager will magically fix all issues without proper testing; always test your association and include safe checks so remediation does not create side effects. The outcome is continuous compliance for network-critical settings with audit trails for each remediation action. State Manager — desired state and remediation means use state manager to continuously enforce and remediate in-instance network configurations according to a declared desired state.. In practical terms, how state manager associations enforce and remediate network configuration drift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › State Manager
Association flow
Create an association tying an SSM Document to a set of instances. Choose schedule or event triggers. State Manager will run the document and report compliance status.
Target by tags or resource groups for flexible scope management.
Choose frequency to balance responsiveness and operational load.
Enable compliance reporting so security teams can see remediations and drift metrics.
Concrete scenario
Ensure bastion hosts have fail2ban and a specific iptables OUTPUT rule blocking 1.2.3.0/24. State Manager runs a document that checks presence and applies the rule if missing, saving the rule persistently.
Common misconception
State Manager will not prevent harmful commands if the document is destructive. Author safe, idempotent documents and test them before associations run broadly.

screens.title: State Manager: schedule, detect drift, and remediate
screens.narratorSegment: Designing an effective State Manager remediation cycle means balancing frequency, scope, and safety. Start by selecting the correct targets — use tags to include only the instances that need the network policy. Next, choose a schedule that checks for drift often enough to be effective but not so often it creates excessive load; for firewall rules a 15- to 30-minute cadence is common, but you should base it on your operational tolerance. The document should first detect current state, report if it’s compliant, and only apply changes if necessary. For remediation, include persistence steps so changes survive reboots, such as writing to sysctl. conf or saving iptables. Log outputs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 so you can inspect remediations. Finally, enable compliance reporting and alerting so unsuccessful remediations or repeated drift generate an operational ticket. A misconception is treating State Manager as a replacement for proper change control: you should still track and approve documents and associations, and test them in non-production before wide rollouts. The result is a controlled, observable loop that keeps network-critical settings consistent. State Manager: schedule, detect drift, and remediate means target precisely, schedule wisely, detect before enforcing, persist changes, and monitor remediations for operational visibility.. In practical terms, design a remediation cycle that keeps network rules consistent across instance lifecycles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: SSM security and IAM best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security is crucial when automating network configuration. The instance profile attached to each EC2 must grant the SSM Agent only the permissions it needs — typically AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore plus specific additional permissions for resources the document requires, such as S3 read for scripts or CloudWatch logging permissions. Avoid granting broad administrative permissions to the instance. Control who can create and execute SSM Documents and associations with IAM policies so only authorized operators or automation pipelines can run network-affecting documents. Prefer Session Manager for interactive troubleshooting because it removes the need to open inbound SSH ports and provides an auditable session log. Always test documents in a non-production environment before deploying widely and include safeguards such as dry-run checks or confirmation steps in automation that could affect connectivity. A common misconception is that SSM is fully safe by default; it is secure when combined with least-privilege IAM, targeted scope, and controlled document execution. Treat SSM as a powerful operational channel that requires governance. SSM security and IAM best practices means grant instance profiles minimal permissions, restrict who can run documents, and prefer session manager for interactive access.. In practical terms, minimize blast radius: instance profiles, document permissions, and session manager for safe access. screens.title: Terminal demo: Use Run Command and verify changes via CLI
screens.narratorSegment: This terminal-style walkthrough consolidates the practical steps you will use in the lab. Start by verifying the EC2 instance is managed by SSM: check Fleet Manager in the console or confirm the SSM Agent is online. With the AWS CLI, send a simple inspection command such as ip a using aws ssm send-command and the AWS-RunShellScript document. Capture the returned CommandId from the response. Next, retrieve the output with aws ssm list-command-invocations --command-id and the --details flag, then query the CommandPlugins output to see the command output. For a configuration change, send a command that runs sudo sysctl -w fs. file-max=100000 or the iptables update, then verify with another invocation. Remember that temporary kernel parameter changes revert on reboot unless you persist them in /etc/sysctl. conf. Always test these commands in a non-production environment first. A key misconception is assuming outputs propagate instantly; allow a short time for the SSM Agent to execute and for results to be available. End your demo by checking CloudTrail or CloudWatch Logs to confirm the action is auditable. This workflow gives you reproducible, auditable steps for network changes without SSH.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Hands-on CLI
Verify SSM managed status
Confirm the instance appears in Fleet Manager or use the CLI to check managed instance inventory before sending commands.
# Send an inspection command
aws ssm send-command \
  --instance-ids "i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
  --document-name "AWS-RunShellScript" \
  --parameters 'commands=["ip a"]' \
  --comment "Check network interface eth0" \
  --output json

# Capture the CommandId from response and then:
aws ssm list-command-invocations \
  --command-id "cmd-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
  --details \
  --query "CommandInvocations[0].CommandPlugins[0].Output" \
  --output text
For a configuration change that must persist, include persistence steps in the script and verify with a follow-up invocation or by checking the file where the setting was saved.
Example change
Increase a kernel parameter temporarily using send-command, then persist it by appending to /etc/sysctl.conf in the same document if desired.
Audit
Check CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs for command execution records to maintain an audit trail of who executed what and the resulting outputs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how AWS Systems Manager becomes the operational plane for network configuration tasks that live inside instances. Systems Manager is different from infrastructure provisioning: it runs inside the managed instance via the SSM Agent, so it’s the right tool when you need to change kernel parameters, update firewall rules, deploy network agents, or keep virtual appliances consistent over time. We’ll explore three core capabilities: Run Command for ad-hoc and scripted remote execution, State Manager for defining and enforcing desired configuration, and Patch Manager for keeping network-related software patched. You will also see how EventBridge and CloudWatch can trigger and monitor SSM actions so automation can be event-driven and observable. Security is central: we’ll review instance profile permissions, how to limit who can run documents, and why Session Manager is safer than opening SSH. You’ll finish with a terminal-style walkthrough showing the CLI calls to send a Run Command, check outputs, and create a State Manager association. By the end, you’ll know which SSM capability fits each operational need and how to automate network changes safely and audibly.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform several practical tasks that solve common network automation needs. First, you will use Run Command to execute scripts or single commands remotely across EC2 instances. This matters because you can change firewall rules or install network agents without opening SSH or manually logging into machines. Second, you will author and deploy State Manager associations to declare desired OS-level network settings and remediate drift automatically. Enforcing state ensures that critical iptables rules or kernel parameters remain present and consistent. Third, you will apply Patch Manager concepts to schedule and verify patching of operating systems and network components so that vulnerabilities that affect network integrity are addressed. Fourth, you’ll start to combine SSM with EventBridge and CloudWatch so that automation becomes event-driven and observable, allowing proactive responses to launches or configuration failures. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can measure practical mastery.

This second objectives slide focuses on the operational and security practices that make SSM safe for network automation. You will learn to verify SSM Agent presence and the instance's managed status as a prerequisite to automation. You will be able to author or reuse SSM Documents safely, understanding parameterization, idempotence, and persistence so that changes survive or do not cause unintended side effects. You will practice validating outputs from send-command calls and using CloudWatch or S3 for storing command results for auditability. Finally, you will adopt a testing workflow: always validate documents in a staging environment, confirm IAM instance profile privileges follow least privilege, and prefer Session Manager for troubleshooting instead of opening SSH. These skills reduce blast radius and help you automate without disrupting network connectivity. Learning Objectives — Security & Practical Skills means combine verification, safe document design, output validation, and least-privilege policies to automate network changes responsibly.. In practical terms, operational checks, documents, and testing you must master. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common confusion is when to use CloudFormation and when to use Systems Manager. CloudFormation is excellent for provisioning AWS resources: VPCs, subnets, security groups, and instance shapes. It is declarative and designed for reproducible infrastructure. However, many network settings live inside the instance operating system or inside virtual appliances running on EC2. These settings include kernel tuning, iptables rules, installed network agents, or software configuration that CloudFormation cannot change after instance boot. Systems Manager operates through the SSM Agent on the instance, giving you an operational channel to execute commands, apply states, and run patching tasks. Use Run Command for one-off or immediate changes across a fleet; use State Manager to declare the desired OS-level state and enforce it over time. A misconception is thinking CloudFormation handles all configuration; in practice, infrastructure as code and in-instance configuration are complementary. For example, you might provision a bastion host with CloudFormation, then use State Manager to ensure fail2ban and iptables rules remain configured. The key takeaway: use the provisioning plane for resources, and the operational plane (SSM) for the configuration that lives inside instances.

Run Command is the Systems Manager capability that lets you execute commands or scripts on one or many managed instances without SSH. It leverages the SSM Agent running on instances and SSM Documents that define the actions to run. AWS ships pre-built documents like AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript, and you can author custom JSON or YAML documents. A typical use case for network operators is updating firewall rules across a fleet. For example, you can push an iptables update to allow SSH only from a trusted CIDR and drop other inbound SSH attempts. When invoking Run Command you target instances by instance ID, tags, or resource groups and choose where to store output, such as CloudWatch Logs or S3. A common mistake is giving overly broad IAM permissions to the instance profile; always restrict the instance profile to the minimum required. Another important practice is to persist changes when necessary — for iptables that might mean calling a distribution-specific save command. Finally, because Run Command is auditable through CloudTrail and log destinations, operations and security teams can trace who ran what and when. In short, Run Command gives safe, scalable, and auditable remote execution for network tasks.

This screen walks through a terminal-style workflow to send and verify a Run Command using the AWS CLI. First, you must ensure the instance is managed by SSM and has an attached instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Then use aws ssm send-command with the AWS-RunShellScript document and specify commands as parameters. The CLI returns a CommandId. Use list-command-invocations with that CommandId and the --details flag to view plugin output and status. Store results in CloudWatch Logs or S3 if you need persistent audit records. A concrete example: send a command that runs ip a or sysctl to inspect network state; then fetch output to confirm the change applied. A common pitfall is not replacing placeholders for instance IDs or CommandId when copying commands — always confirm identifiers. Also be aware that some changes require root privileges or distribution-specific persistence steps; include those in your script. Finally, avoid opening SSH ports for this workflow: Run Command operates over the secure SSM channel, reducing exposure in your network security groups. Run Command — CLI workflow and verifying output means send command, record commandid, and fetch commandinvocations with details to validate outputs and success.. In practical terms, walk through the send-command, check status, and retrieve output using the aws cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An SSM Document is a JSON or YAML file that defines the actions Systems Manager performs on managed instances. Documents can be commands, automations, or policies that call actions such as aws:runShellScript. AWS supplies many pre-built documents like AWS-RunShellScript, but for network automation you will often author custom documents to parameterize IP ranges, file paths, or sysctl keys. Safe authoring practices include parameterization to avoid hard-coded values, idempotent commands so repeated runs do not cause unintended state changes, and explicit persistence when changes must survive reboots. For example, a document that sets a sysctl key should check the current value, write the new value if needed, and append to /etc/sysctl. conf so the setting persists. Test documents in a staging environment and include logging and error checks to avoid network disruption. Also be mindful of required permissions: some documents need S3 or CloudWatch access for scripts and output locations; grant only the minimum permissions necessary. By designing documents that validate before changing and report clear outcomes, you reduce risk when automating network configuration. SSM Documents — structure and authoring best practices means author documents that are parameterized, idempotent, and include persistence and logging to minimize operational risk.. In practical terms, what an ssm document is, document types, and safe authoring patterns for network tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

State Manager lets you declare and enforce a desired state on a group of instances by associating an SSM Document to target instances and a schedule or trigger. Think of it as a watchdog that checks and repairs instance-level settings: it runs the document you provide on the targets and, on schedule or when drift is detected, re-applies the steps to bring instances back to the desired state. This is ideal for ensuring firewalls, fail2ban configurations, kernel parameters, or the presence of network tools remain consistent. When creating an association, define targeting by tags or resource groups, choose a schedule frequency, and set compliance reporting so teams can monitor remediations. A practical example is enforcing an iptables rule that blocks a malicious subnet: the State Manager document checks for the rule and reapplies it if missing. Misconceptions include thinking State Manager will magically fix all issues without proper testing; always test your association and include safe checks so remediation does not create side effects. The outcome is continuous compliance for network-critical settings with audit trails for each remediation action. State Manager — desired state and remediation means use state manager to continuously enforce and remediate in-instance network configurations according to a declared desired state.. In practical terms, how state manager associations enforce and remediate network configuration drift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down.
